body:
It seems you're using regex to get all the values wrapped in double quotes? This likely won't work since the parser parses out a single parameter value from the line

e.g.

This is parsed as `parameters[stop]=[]string{"foo"}`
```
PARAMETER stop "foo" "bar" "baz"
```

While this is parsed as `parameters[stop]=[]string{"foo bar baz"}`
```
PARAMETER stop foo "bar baz"
```

Clearly this is the wrong behaviour but implementing a parser that can handle this correctly is not worthwhile right now. 

What I have in mind is something like this to create `parameters[stop]=[]string{"foo", "bar baz"}`

```
PARAMETER stop foo
PARAMETER stop "bar baz"
```

This won't work immediately either since values are inserted into a `map[string]string` so the last value will override all previous values

```
FROM ./ollama-model-f16.bin QUANTIZE Q4_0

body:
First of all thanks for your effort here, I can see from PR #7097 that you do polished work on the OS X side of things.
That PR should be merged as it's a good platform-specific change on a platform specific installer. 

Now this PR is a bit different as it has a very "Mac User" wording and orientation; what do I mean? Well take a look at this from your change:

```
...prompt you for administrative access in order to install
the command line executable, which in practice means symlinking 
`/Applications/Ollama.app/Contents/Resources/ollama`...
```
^^^^^^^ <- See that `Applications/Ollama/Contents`, these are all Mac OSX concerns, not linux at all, and certainly not windows, the point is, if you're going to do this, then "Do it well", Do it for all three platforms in a nice bulleted or sectioned style.

1.) The Mac OSX install is a zip that opens into an app, that when executed asks to move itself into the Applications folder, and then tells the user what it's doing and then tells the user what command to run in the terminal. It's the "Tesla Autopilot" version of all the Ollama installs.

2.) Windows is similar, you are guided through it step by step, but windows command line stuff is inherently harder due to the ambiguity of powershell vs WSL terminal and because WSL can access windows filesystem and do stuff so people often just use WSL to do terminal things. See what I mean? It's more complicated on windows.

3.) Now the linux install is fairly straightforward, but no GUI popups flash in front of the user, guiding them step-by-step on how to use Ollama. It could use some sprucing up, like "Hey here is where the models are kept, here is the file linking those weird sha looking files to the actual model names, etc" We don't have to tell them (though it's an excellent idea) where the systemctl ollama.service file is, but if we did and showed them how to add/remove environment variable lines and change startup options for ollama, that would actually be super helpful.

Now if you took the installation section and subdivided it into each of those 3 platforms, and then did a fairly decent job on each one, that would actually be awesome work and we could iterate on that and polish it.

If not, then it's better not to selectively document a single platform while neglecting the others. I can see how the reviewer would suggest that this type of platform specific documentation be located in a "getting started" style documentation guide, that would move it out of the main readme.md and let the technical writer develop the install docs without having to worry about keeping readme.md tidy, they could then go 100% and really document the install for all three platforms.

So yeah, makes alot of sense to do that, and cover all three platforms while doing so.

body:
This is a huge improvement.

I've seen some issues here with concurrent downloads. 
1) Downloading from multiple clients which cancel and resume may result in an incorrect check-sum.
My stress test:
   - pull in client A
   - pull in client B
   - pull in client C
   - cancel client A
   - cancel client B
   - cancel client C
   - resume and finish A, checksum error
2) concurrent pulls result in the second pull getting stuck when multiple files are downloaded:
```
./ollama pull falcon
pulling manifest
pulling 3230a638a2da... 100% |███████| (4.2/4.2 GB, 70 MB/s)
pulling d5311aab7c4c...   0% |                     | ( 0/ 0 B) [0s:0s]
```
My other client finished pulling while this one was stuck here.

I think only problem `2)` is really a blocker for the time being, and seems like it might just be a logic tweak.

This is the maximum chunk size. The chunk size is the lower of this value and the remaining number of bytes. 

> it can be larger in the case of a partial download (the offset)?

I don't understand what this is ask. A chunk starts at offset and stops at offset+size. This is configuring a new chunk so start and stop are well defined. When resuming a download, a chunk starts at offset+completed and ends at offset+size where completed < size.

body:
Building these separate runners is showing the limits of how we use `go generate`. There ends up being a lot of layers of indirection, `go generate -> go logic -> build and run shell commands from go`. Let's take this opportunity to simplify and move this logic to a shell script, I whipped this up based on your logic in here:
```
#!/bin/sh

# Set ROCM path from environment variable or default to /opt/rocm
ROCM_PATH="${ROCM_PATH:-/opt/rocm}"

# Check for CUDA and generate for GGUF and GGML
if nvcc &>/dev/null; then
    echo "Building with CUDA"

    cmake -S gguf -B gguf/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_CUBLAS=on
    cmake --build gguf/build/cuda --target server --config Release

    cmake -S ggml -B ggml/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_CUBLAS=on
    cmake --build ggml/build/cuda --target server --config Release

# Check for ROCM and generate for GGUF
elif [ -d "$ROCM_PATH" ]; then
    echo "Building with ROCM"

    # GGML does not support ROCM, only generate GGUF
    cmake -S gguf -B gguf/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_HIPBLAS=on -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=$ROCM_PATH/llvm/bin/clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=$ROCM_PATH/llvm/bin/clang++
    cmake --build gguf/build/cuda --target server --config Release

# Check for OpenCL and generate for GGUF and GGML
elif clinfo &>/dev/null; then
    echo "Building with OpenCL"

    cmake -S gguf -B gguf/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_CLBLAST=on
    cmake --build gguf/build/cuda --target server --config Release

    cmake -S ggml -B ggml/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_CLBLAST=on
    cmake --build ggml/build/cuda --target server --config Release

else
    echo "No GPU found, skipping GPU build"
fi
```

The in the `generate_linux.go` we can just call this shell script for now and keep the cuda building logic in the shell script:
```
diff --git a/llm/llama.cpp/generate_linux.go b/llm/llama.cpp/generate_linux.go
index 4cae384..d0d7be0 100644
--- a/llm/llama.cpp/generate_linux.go
+++ b/llm/llama.cpp/generate_linux.go
@@ -16,7 +16,4 @@ package llm
 //go:generate cmake -S gguf -B gguf/build/cpu -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on
 //go:generate cmake --build gguf/build/cpu --target server --config Release
 
-//go:generate cmake -S ggml -B ggml/build/cuda -DLLAMA_CUBLAS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on
-//go:generate cmake --build ggml/build/cuda --target server --config Release
-//go:generate cmake -S gguf -B gguf/build/cuda -DLLAMA_CUBLAS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on
-//go:generate cmake --build gguf/build/cuda --target server --config Release
+//go:generate sh cuda.sh
```

`deleteMap` is a reference counter for unused layer. On creation, a layer may be unused if the new tag overrides the previous tag. Adding a layer to `deleteMap` signals the layer may be dangling after creation if it's not referenced by other models.

e.g. model A has layers a, b, c. User creates a new model from A, also called A, overriding layer b with d. Layer b is now dangling and should be removed.

I've tried a couple possibilities, but no solution yet...

Turns out there's a `/usr/local/cuda/lib64/stubs/libnvidia-ml.so` in WSL2 if you have the CUDA libs installed, but at runtime that fails with a wall of text error and code:
```
NVML_ERROR_DRIVER_NOT_LOADED = 9
NVIDIA driver is not loaded.
```

I also found `/mnt/c/Windows/System32/lxss/lib/libnvidia-ml.so.1` is present, however that also fails at runtime with an init error of:
```
NVML_ERROR_OPERATING_SYSTEM = 17
The GPU control device has been blocked by the operating system/cgroups.
```
(root or normal user doesn't matter)

That last error feels like it might be solvable if we can figure out how things are wired up, but I'm not sure.

My inclination would be to merge what we've got and note this as a limitation on WSL2 for the pre-release (Your call @jmorganca ). I imagine a lot of people running in WSL2 will be happier with it running natively, which it does in its current form.  We can continue to investigate if there's a viable solution to get libnvidia-ml.so to load inside WSL2, and if not, fallback to the CLI as @BruceMacD suggested.

body: The CUDA based built-in should be able to fallback to CPU, so we don't have to ship this CPU-only build as part of the official release. LLaVA is better at understanding the context of text and images and using that information to answer questions or generate text than Llama2.

if my sample.txt file is:

C'est l'histoire d'un petit chat qui chantait "miaou miaou" tout le temps.

And translate it also in Italian

if my prompt is :

ollama run llama2 --verbose please translate in spanish "$(cat /Users/igor/sample.txt)"

The answer will be:

Spanish: "Es la historia de un pequeño gato que cantaba 'miau miau' todo el tiempo."

Italian: "Questa è la storia di un gattino che cantava 'miao miao' sempre."

The text in the sample.txt file is sent to Ollama and is interpreted as being part of the prompt, not part of the file that must be processed.

By separating the text from the prompt, LLaVA can focus on processing the text content independently, leading to more efficient and accurate responses. This approach could be particularly useful for tasks that require extensive text processing, such as translation or summarization.

body:
The problem this is aiming to solve is dll dependencies.  I wanted to try to keep the main ollama.exe dependent on almost nothing so it would run without any special path setup.  Even the CPU-based llama.cpp has a hand-full of DLLs that need to get loaded, and if they aren't in the path, and we link the way we were at Go compile time, then the resulting ollama.exe would simply fail to start without any useful error message.

This allows me to augment the PATH at runtime while loading these libraries so the user doesn't have to deal with the complexities of finding the dependencies.  Instead, we can carry them as payloads and store them in the temp dir.

CPU-only inference works on my Pixel 7 pro (aarch64) using update-to-date Termux (F-Droid) running on top of GrapheneOS (based on AOSP Android 14). So far, I've had decent success (albeit slow) with the legacy q4 and q5 formats but K_S & K_M not so much. It will be nice if working Vulkan and/or TPU support can eventually be added. Otherwise, without `RTLD_DEEPBIND`, the build succeeds and the dynamic CPU module loads successfully.

It also opens the question of if we should also try to use the libcudart.so we carry as payload: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/llm/generate/gen_linux.sh#L148-L157
> 
> If this turns out to be reliable for gathering GPU information, we could consider dropping the nvidia-ml dependency entirely.

@dhiltgen I can work on that. Could you please provide some clarification on this though:

routes.go seems to call the initializer for llm.go (llm.Init()), which calls payload_common.go, and has it looking up which libraries are present on the host system. Based on that, it requests the necessary llama.cpp server bundles, then unpackages the libraries included in the server bundle into the /tmp/ollama######## folder it creates, and prints which libraries were loaded.

routes.go
[https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/routes.go#L987-L998](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/routes.go#L987-L998)

llm.go
[https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/llm/llm.go#L145-L157](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/llm/llm.go#L145-L157)

payload_common.go
[https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/llm/payload_common.go#L105-L149](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/llm/payload_common.go#L105-L149)

The clarification I am requesting is this seems like a chicken and egg scenario: gpu.go finds libraries on host to determine if can load CUDA, ROCM, Metal, or CPU, then it unbundles the relevant package and loads that library on the backend. payload_common extracts payloads but doesn't return anything of use to its calling functions. 

TL;DR: using the bundled libraries is a great idea but would require re-working how gpu.go is initialized.

Agreed, we'll need to reshuffle things a bit to fully realize that approach.  I think we can break this down into ~3 different steps.

1. What I think makes the most sense is to first refactor this "tegra" code to be a "cuda" variant that will work on tegra and plain old cuda linux/windows systems where nvidial-ml didn't work or wasn't found.  Initially, start with just the cudart lib found on the host, and I think that would be a mergeable state for this PR .
2. Then an incremental follow up PR could reshuffle the library extraction flow so that we can add the cudart payload into the search path at the end, and move this cuda based lookup before nvidial-ml
3. Finally, if things are looking good and people aren't hitting problems, we can remove the nvidial-ml lookup.

I haven't had as much time to work on this as I'd like, but I have made progress.

Running into an issue with the way free memory is reported on Tegra devices. It seems like the OS already builds in a kind of "buffer" into it's reported free memory, and it's fairly significant. I'm going to remove the artificial buffer for Tegra devices and see if I run into any issues.

![image](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/assets/105550370/44004264-834f-4696-b337-abb69ceb0d1f)

![image](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/assets/105550370/0c794df0-8265-4f5a-a4d2-142bcd06d590)

As shown in the screenshots, quite a big variance in reported free memory, resulting in layers not being properly sent to GPU as shown here:

![image](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/assets/105550370/79ed97fd-c3cc-431f-b761-5ae59b2d964f)

Note: this started happening after loading a 2nd model. I initially loaded Mistral 7b and it worked just fine. When I switched to openhermes, that's when it stopped sending all the layers to GPU. I think for Tegra devices, we can probably let the L4T OS handle the extra buffer and just report 100% of the free memory reported by CUDA or the system versus adding the 1GB or 10% buffer.

body:
Tegra has a caching system it uses that eats up "available memory" but is ready to be freed on demand. When I left in the 1024MB overhead, it would frequently give "falling back to CPU -> OOM" even though JTOP was showing enough memory free. I tried to find an automated system to properly report available memory to include freeable cache and the gist is that "free -m" produces the most accurate (and accurate is almost an incorrect word) depiction of free memory in Linux and should be what is used. There isn't a library or API to query the same data other than reading it directly from /proc (and in fact, that's what the `free` binary does). 

TL;DR I let the Tegra OS manage overhead as it seems to be better at it than me. Also the reported memory from the sysinfo library, the cuda driver free memory reported, and jtop were all inconsistent in the values reported.

body:
It is used to see if the model currently loaded into memory needs to be changed still:
```
// load a model into memory if it is not already loaded, it is up to the caller to lock loaded.mu before calling this function
func load(c *gin.Context, model *Model, opts api.Options, sessionDuration time.Duration) error {
	workDir := c.GetString("workDir")

	needLoad := loaded.runner == nil || // is there a model loaded?
		loaded.ModelPath != model.ModelPath || // has the base model changed?
		!reflect.DeepEqual(loaded.AdapterPaths, model.AdapterPaths) || // have the adapters changed?
		!reflect.DeepEqual(loaded.Options.Runner, opts.Runner) // have the runner options changed?

	if needLoad {
		if loaded.runner != nil {
			slog.Info("changing loaded model")
			loaded.runner.Close()
			loaded.runner = nil
			loaded.Model = nil
			loaded.Options = nil
		}
```

author: rick-github

body:
This is an excellent comment. In this case, the base image is Ubuntu:

$ docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/sh ollama/ollama
# cat /etc/lsb-release
DISTRIB_ID=Ubuntu
DISTRIB_RELEASE=22.04
DISTRIB_CODENAME=jammy
DISTRIB_DESCRIPTION="Ubuntu 22.04.3 LTS"

Which means, that the system shell /usr/bin/sh is linked to dash

# ls -l /usr/bin/sh
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 4 Mar 23  2022 /usr/bin/sh -> dash

Testing with the system shell (dash) indeed does not support the /dev/tcp mechanism for creating TCP connections:

# cat < /dev/null > /dev/tcp/localhost/11434
/bin/sh: 7: cannot create /dev/tcp/localhost/11434: Directory nonexistent
# echo $?
2

However using bash, we are able to support this health-check:

# bash
root@0026649d68b2:/# cat < /dev/null > /dev/tcp/localhost/11434
root@0026649d68b2:/# echo $?
0

Thus, we should be specifying bash explicitly in the compose yml file, with the health-check. 

SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]

Which I'll add to the configuration. 

Thanks again for this insightful comment!
author: jmcdice

body:
Just a further comment after additional investigation, indeed the health-check fails using the original configuration:

$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE           COMMAND               CREATED              STATUS                          PORTS                                           NAMES
075df43c3f46   ollama/ollama   "/bin/ollama serve"   About a minute ago   Up About a minute (unhealthy)   0.0.0.0:11434->11434/tcp, :::11434->11434/tcp   ollama

Notice (unhealth). 

Changing the health-check to explicitly use bash in the compose file, returns a healthy status:

      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/usr/bin/bash -c 'cat < /dev/null > /dev/tcp/localhost/${OLLAMA_PORT:-11434} || exit 1'"]
      
Returns a successful (healthy) status:

$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE           COMMAND               CREATED         STATUS                   PORTS                                           NAMES
7b0498b23ea4   ollama/ollama   "/bin/ollama serve"   2 minutes ago   Up 2 minutes (healthy)   0.0.0.0:11434->11434/tcp, :::11434->11434/tcp   ollama

So, again - great call out.

I don't believe it's possible to trigger a build on a draft release.  The flow we're thinking is:

1. [Optional] Create a draft release specifying the intended tag, author the draft release notes, etc.
2. Git tag and push the tag 
3. CI triggers at this point, and builds all the artifacts, then uploads them idempotently to the pre-existing release (if you did step 1)
4. Smoke/spot test the artifacts to verify things are good (eventually we'll automate this)
5. Update to Pre-release (drop draft status)
6. Broader testing
7. Mark release latest / drop pre-release.

body:
The libraries copied to the ${BUILD_DIR}/bin directory contain the essential oneAPI dependencies required for running the llama.cpp. There's no need for users to install oneAPI themselves, as the build system handles this dependency which means build system should install oneAPI.

When the ollama binary executes, these dependencies are extracted to a temporary location on the user's machine. Upon detecting an Intel GPU driver, we appends the path to this temporary directory (containing the oneAPI dependencies) to the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable. This ensures that even if oneAPI isn't installed locally, the program can still locate the necessary libraries to function.

body:
Good question.  

For NVIDIA GPUs, we use their C libraries to discover the GPUs.  We've recently switched to using the Driver API as our primary source, and fall back to the cuda runtime library if that fails (most likely we'll remove the cuda runtime code in a few releases as long as the Driver API looks reliable)  Those libraries already implement filtering based on this environment variable, so the calls [here ](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/gpu/gpu_info_nvcuda.c#L87) and [here ](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/gpu/gpu_info_cudart.c#L85) will only return a subset of GPUs based on that variable if the user has set it.

In our scheduler, we pick which GPU (of the GPUs exposed) to run a model on, and when we run the subprocess for inference, we wire up the environment variable to ensure that subprocess uses exactly the set of GPUs we want it to use.

body:
# Code Review: Install Script - Add Environment File Support

## Overview
This change improves the systemd service configuration by adding support for loading environment variables from `/etc/default/ollama`. A default environment file is created during installation with commented examples of common OLLAMA_* configuration options.

---

## Analysis

### Changes Summary

1. **Service Configuration** (`[Service]` section):
   - Added `EnvironmentFile=/etc/default/ollama` directive
   - Added `ExecStartPre` check to log when env file loads successfully

2. **Installation Script**:
   - Added conditional creation of `/etc/default/ollama` if it doesn't exist
   - Creates pre-populated file with commented example settings:
     - `OLLAMA_MODELS`: Model storage location
     - `OLLAMA_HOST`: Listening address and port
     - `OLLAMA_ORIGINS`: CORS allowed origins
     - `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODEL`: Max concurrent loaded models
     - `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL`: Parallel request handling

---

## Strengths

1. **Linux Best Practice**: Following the `/etc/default/<service>` convention is standard on Debian/Ubuntu systems. Users familiar with this pattern will find it intuitive.

2. **Non-Breaking Default**: The script only creates the file if it doesn't exist, preserving any existing custom configurations.

3. **Clear Documentation**: Commented examples in the file serve as inline documentation for available configuration options.

4. **Logging Improvement**: `ExecStartPre` logs when the environment file is loaded, aiding debugging for operators.

5. **Path Pre-Setting Preserved**: Existing `Environment="PATH=$PATH"` remains, maintaining compatibility.

---

## Considerations

### 1. **File Permissions Security**

```bash
sudo bash -c "cat <<EOF > $FILE"
```

**Current behavior**: Creates file with root permissions (700) since command runs as sudo.

**Recommendation**: Explicitly set restrictive permissions to prevent unauthorized modification of sensitive environment variables:

```bash
echo "... content ..." | sudo tee "$FILE" >/dev/null && sudo chmod 600 "$FILE"
chmod 600 "$FILE"  # After file is created
```

Without proper permissions, any local user could potentially read sensitive values like API keys if they're stored there.

### 2. **Variable Expansion in Heredoc**

The heredoc uses quotes around `<<EOF` which prevents variable expansion. This is correct and intentional since we want literal variable names in the config file. No changes needed here.

### 3. **Existing Environment Conflicts**

If `/etc/default/ollama` already exists with different variables than system defaults, systemd may report conflicts. Consider:

```bash
if [ -f "$FILE" ]; then
    echo "Existing environment file detected at $FILE"
    echo "Modifications can be made manually before restarting the service"
fi
```

### 4. **Environment Precedence**

systemd processes `Environment` and `EnvironmentFile` in a specific order. Verify that `EnvironmentFile` variables don't unintentionally override important system-level `Environment` settings. Document precedence in the file comments.

### 5. **Heredoc Indentation**

The heredoc appears indented within the shell script block. Ensure the `$FILE` variable inside is expanded correctly. Test that the resulting file has no unintended leading whitespace.

---

## Potential Issues

| Issue | Severity | Mitigation |
|-------|----------|------------|
| World-readable env file | High | Set `chmod 600` after creation |
| Permission escalation attack | Medium | Validate env file ownership stays `root:root` |
| Config syntax errors not caught until reboot | Low | Add validation step after creation |
| Existing users lose access to current configs | Low | Preserve existing files (already handled) |
| Missing newline at EOF | Low | Ensure heredoc ends cleanly |

---

## Testing Recommendations

### 1. **Permission Verification**
```bash
#!/bin/bash
# After running install.sh
stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/default/ollama
# Expected: 600 root:root
```

### 2. **Config Override Test**
```bash
# Pre-create file with different settings
sudo mkdir -p /etc/default
echo 'OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434' | sudo tee /etc/default/ollama

# Run installer
./install.sh --system

# Verify existing config preserved
grep "OLLAMA_HOST" /etc/default/ollama
```

### 3. **Service Start Test**
```bash
# After installation
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ollama

# Check env file was loaded
sudo systemctl show ollama | grep -i environment
```

### 4. **Edge Case Tests**
- Fresh install on minimal container image
- Upgrade from previous version with existing env vars
- Install on non-standard filesystem paths
- Multiple concurrent installs

---

## Documentation Updates Needed

1. **Install Notes**: Document that env vars can now be customized via `/etc/default/ollama`

2. **Example Snippets**: Provide copy-paste ready examples:
   ```bash
   # Set GPU offloading
   cat >> /etc/default/ollama << EOF
   OLLAMA_MODELS=/mnt/storage/models
   OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1
   EOF
   
   sudo systemctl reload-or-restart ollama
   ```

3. **Systemd Integration Guide**: Explain interaction between `Environment` and `EnvironmentFile`

4. **Security Warning**: Note that sensitive values in the env file are world-readable without proper permissions

---

## Recommendation: Approve with Minor Revisions

This is a well-designed enhancement that improves the service's configurability and aligns with Linux best practices. The fix is backward-compatible and low-risk.

**Actions Required Before Merge:**

1. ✅ **Add permission hardening**:
   ```bash
   if [ ! -f "$FILE" ]; then
       sudo bash -c "cat <<EOF > $FILE
   ...config...
   EOF"
       sudo chmod 600 "$FILE"  # CRITICAL SECURITY FIX
       sudo chown root:root "$FILE"  # Ensure ownership
   fi
   ```

2. ✅ **Add comment about security implications** at top of template file

3. ✅ **Test all installation scenarios** (fresh install, upgrade, existing config)

4. ✅ **Verify systemd reload behavior** on existing installations

body:
The previous code changed when the include the output tensor. When using Metal with mmap, the output layer is counted first before any repeating layers are counted. When not using Metal or mmap is disabled, the output layer is counted last after all repeating layers are counted.

There's a bug upstream for macOS with mmap enabled where memory is allocated based on a layer's file offset. If an unrelated tensor is interleaved with a layer, it will include the tensor despite not actually being offloaded. This happens most frequently with the output tensor but it can realistically happen to any tensor or entire repeating layers

body:
There is a defect on this line.

This defect can be triggered with the following BNF. The parser does not consider the `]` at the end of the first character class (`[^"\\]`) to be properly terminating, and therefore interprets everything up until the next `]` as part of this character class. So the parser produces the token "{ Type: TokenCharacterClass, Value `[^"\\] | "\\" (["\\/bfnrt]` }", which creates downstream issues in this case (it later errors with "unmatched closing parenthesis").
```bnf
string-char ::= [^"\\] | "\\" (["\\/bfnrt] | "u" [0-9a-fA-F] [0-9a-fA-F] [0-9a-fA-F] [0-9a-fA-F])
```

I believe the six different scenarios are: `]`, `\]`, `\\]`, plus the same three scenarios at the beginning of the string. However, only `\]` should not terminate the character class. I believe, from my local testing, the correct condition is:

```go
if rule[i] == ']' && (i == 0 || rule[i-1] != '\\' || (i > 1 && rule[i-2] == '\\')) {
```

Also, doesn't this break the current behavior? If I'm used to this flag only changing `https` to `http` and now it does not do that, and instead skips TLS verification without rewriting the scheme, that is not the behavior I would expect. I would want it to push to the http endpoint or none at all, not skip TLS verification.

If that is not what is happening, my bad, but maybe we need to rethink the docs here. If it is what is happening, then: 

I'd like to preempt any "Insecure is insecure" counterpoints with: "This is a breaking change." and propose we simply update the `-insecure` flag with more thought. See proposal in comment below.
author: bmizerany

body:
What happens if I set this _and_ `-insecure`? Is it a nop, an error? It's confusing to have these two flags. It's always confusing to have flags that get canceled out, silently, by another.

I would also be unfortunate to have the two flags, when they could be one, and without breaking the existing behavior that `-insecure` has today.

A (very serious) proposal:

Change the flag to be  _set_ (or simply present), like: `-insecure[="https-only" | "http-only" | "skip-verify"]`. The rules are:

- If present but without a value (e.g. `-insecure`) it defaults to http-only, which is the behavior today.
- If present and set, do what the value says
- If not present, default to `https-only`

The values mean:

- `https-only`: Use HTTPS, always verify TLS
- `skip-verify`: Use HTTPS, but skip TLS verification
- `http-only`: Use HTTP, only. There is no TLS to skip or verify.

> NOTE: The https-only value is there for completeness and should be allowed as a value even though it could be "set" but not using the flag at all.

This is not the most ideal situation to be in, I know. However, the flag was unfortunately introduced to mean something other that "skip TLS verification", so here we are.

In conclusion, the above proposal allows us to maintain the current behavior/meaning of the `-insecure` flag, and allows us to avoid introducing an admittedly ambiguous and confusing `-http` flag.

The best way to close a file is to defer right after open succeeds, e.g.

```go
f, err := os.Open(p)
if err != nil {
  return nil, err
}
defer f.Close()
```

This ensure the file is closed even when the function returns early, e.g. DecodeGGML errors

In general, my goal is for this to be a temporary flag that is eventually replaced by an implementation that is either general to all cases or is self tuning. It was intentionally left undocumented so that we aren't committing to it.

One of the problems with this type of config (besides users not knowing what to do) is that it will probably be hard to set appropriately in all but the most straightforward of cases. Real environments will have a mix of situations where different cache behaviors might be ideal. As a result, the setting is mostly useful for experimentation.

As a result, I'm a little bit hesitant to group this into a larger bucket of config since it likely makes it even more impossible to turn on and get the expected results.

body:
Should this section mirror the outer logic with regard to `sudo` like so?

```bash
#!/bin/bash

set -eu

TMPFILE=$(mktemp -t ollama_uninstallXXXX.log)

status() { echo ">>> $*" >&2; }
error() { echo "ERROR $*"; exit 1; }
warning() { echo "WARNING: $*"; }

status "Uninstalling ollama. Logs are in ${TMPFILE}"

function run_redirect() {
    echo "Running: '$*'" >> ${TMPFILE} 2>&1
    $* >> ${TMPFILE}  2>&1
    echo "" >> ${TMPFILE}  2>&1
}

SUDO=
if [ "$(id -u)" -ne 0 ]; then
    # Running as root, no need for sudo
    if ! command -v sudo >/dev/null; then
        error "This script requires superuser permissions. Please re-run as root."
    fi
    SUDO="sudo"
fi

run_redirect $SUDO systemctl stop ollama 
run_redirect $SUDO systemctl disable ollama
run_redirect $SUDO rm /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service

OLLAMA_PATH=$(command -v ollama || true)
UNINSTALL_SCRIPT_PATH=$(command -v ollama_uninstall.sh || true)

if [ -n "$OLLAMA_PATH" ]; then
    run_redirect $SUDO rm $OLLAMA_PATH
fi

if [ -n "$UNINSTALL_SCRIPT_PATH" ]; then
    run_redirect $SUDO rm $UNINSTALL_SCRIPT_PATH
fi

run_redirect $SUDO rm -r /usr/share/ollama
run_redirect $SUDO userdel ollama || true
run_redirect $SUDO groupdel ollama || true

status "Uninstall completed"
```

The experience here isn't quite right. I have two main issues.

1. The messages from the previous conversation should still be displayed in the CLI on load. This way I get the context of the current conversation.
```
# interactive chat on this branch
> ollama run mario
>>> 

# interactive chat on main
❯ ollama run mario
>>> lets pretend you are mario from super mario bros
WOOHOO! IT'S-A ME, MARIO!

>>>
```

2. It is a really common pattern with chats to keep the chat state in a slice that keeps getting appended to and using that to display the ongoing conversation. Considering this (and preserving the experience for 1) we should have some way to detect if the incoming messages start with the messages from the Modelfile, and by-pass appending them to the start of the conversation history if so.

This trims spaces outside of quotations. For example :

```
TEMPLATE """{{ if .System }}<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>

{{ .System }}<|eot_id|>{{ end }}{{ if .Prompt }}<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>

{{ .Prompt }}<|eot_id|>{{ end }}<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

{{ .Response }}<|eot_id|>"""      
``` 
has 4 spaces after the `'''`. That will be trimmed. If it's within the quotes, it will take the string literal. 
```
TEMPLATE """{{ if .System }}<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>

{{ .System }}<|eot_id|>{{ end }}{{ if .Prompt }}<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>

{{ .Prompt }}<|eot_id|>{{ end }}<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

{{ .Response }}<|eot_id|>    """
``` 
will not be trimmed

Is this how we want the change to be made?

body:
We can simplify this: instead of the client having to copy the file, let's make the server read it directly. The reason this is important:

* Multi-file input (e.g. safetensor files) will be much faster if the server can read them directly
* What if the cli can't access the model directory due to permissions? (e.g. on Linux) the server will end up having the final say as to whether a file is safely read

Why don't we try this:

1. Client makes a `POST /api/blobs/<blob sha>` with the body as today. However it also provides a header `X-Ollama-File` with the absolute path to the file.
2. The server first tries to read this path, and responds immediately with a 204 if its created
author: jmorganca

body:
Is verifying a full signature required here? I think there are simpler ways:

1. Check `127.0.0.1` or `::1`, verify `Origin`, `Host` and other values are either not set or set to `127.0.0.1`
2. Drop a random secret string in a known location `/tmp/<random id>` directory and send it in the request. Server verifies it before reading the file. This verifies that the client and server have access to the same filesystem.


The problem with the signature on Linux is that `ollama serve` has a different key than the user anyways

body:
It appears that iGPU has sometimes index `1`, not always have index `0`, even if host does not have any other GPUs.

Therefore it may be better just take first line from first file with lowest number:
```suggestion
	cmd := "head -q -n 1 /sys/kernel/debug/dri/[0-9]/i915_gem_objects | head -n 1 | awk '{n=NF-1; print $n}'"
```

Note: while `i915_gem_objects` file first line content has changed over the years, total amount of used memory has always been in the second last field (`n=FN-1`).  If relying on that is not enough, awk in above could replaced with (suitable quoted) sed: `sed -e 's/^.* \([0-9]\+\) bytes$/\1/'`

I understand way too little about building Ollama. But llama.cpp just merged my llama.cpp pull request #8531. 

a) It describes how to build llama.cpp for Windows on ARM. You have to use clang (probably best instlled via the VS2022 installer together with MSVC) and the CMake preset arm64-windows-llvm-release. All in order to support the major acceleration (2-3x prompt-processing, and also some for token-generation) via Q4_0_4_8 quantization. 

b) With my PR, MSVC no longer breaks llama.cpp on WoA-compiles, but it does not support the Q4_0_4_8 acceleration on Snapdragon X.

c) Currently openMP on WoA is manual+shaky, so for now please also use -D GGML_OPENMP=OFF for the llama.cpp build-script. max-krasnyansky and fmz are working on a threadpool update to fix this.

P.S: As Ollama user (besides llama.cpp), I really look forward to your work. Please tell me, if I can support you.

body:
I'll improve the comments to explain it better.

`pickBestFitGPUs` already is [brand aware](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/server/sched.go#L686), and only returns a list of GPUs if the model completely fits into memory.  If it can't find a single brand collection of GPUs that fully fit, it returns nil.  This informs the scheduler that we're in a scenario where some other model has to be unloaded to make room, or this is the first model load.  It's that last case which was the bug this PR is fixing.  For first model load, if the model doesn't fully fit into one brand collection of GPUs, then we'd fall through to a chunk of code that wound up passing the whole list of GPUs with mixed brands into the prediction and server startup logic.

> perhaps we should sort and take the one with the most VRAM?

The `pickBestPartialByLibrary` tries all the brands and picks the one that is able to fit the largest amount of the model.

We _may_ remove these two fields later: `.Config` is an unnecessarily-nested json blob, and I don't think `.SchemaVersion` is (or should be) used.

body:
You are correct that SchemaVersion is not used anywhere currently - it is a write only field. The current version is v2 and this dates back to the first commit - was some there some history that required a version bump from v1? If we are comfortable that we would always just version breaking changes by introducing new field names then we might as well remove it now and stop including it in newly published models. There would be no backwards compatibility issues.

From Config the only field that we use is Digest, which is used to find the config file. Of the fields in that file (which are things like arch, parameters, quantization, etc.), we do use them but mostly in response to commands like ollama show and I assume on the website. They are not actually needed for running the models as the GGUF files include essentially the same metadata. That being said, I don't think there is a good reason to try to de-duplicate these fields - it may limit our flexibility to use other model formats in the future.
author: jessegross

body:
Thanks for hunting that down. That sounds good, it makes sense to remove the check for `SchemaVersion`

Leaving the check for config is okay for now, however I do wonder if we could instead effectively treat it as an optional field and fail gracefully when we try to access it via `.Config.Digest` elsewhere in the code (vs making it a hard required field here on pull, etc).

That would give us a chance to deprecate it later if we wanted to without breaking today's version of Ollama (the general idea going forward would be to put metadata in the manifest object itself vs in a `.Config` "layer" since it's redundant to have to go fetch another layer for a basic json object). Let me know if that makes sense

body:
Here's another try that addresses the following issues:
 * Cleans up the error messages
 * Removes SchemaVersion (both the check and writing it at all in new manifests)
 * Allows .Config to be missing, with just the loss of some information printed in ollama show

The last one has a few caveats if we actually do remove the config from a layer and put it into the manifest file itself. However, none of them are worse than the alternatives - in those cases, we wouldn't be able to make this change at all.
 * Clients that predate this patch (i.e. all of them today) will crash as it will trigger the bug as originally reported here. Obviously we can put the config in both places for a while to stage the rollout and eventually old versions will be thoroughly obsolete anyways.
 * For clients that are new enough to not crash but old enough to not understand the new manifest format, there can be some information loss if they download and then re-upload a model.

Lastly, code-wise this is a little ugly with a bunch of checks for missing config scattered around. I changed the struct so that it is not a pointer so Ollama won't crash if a check is missed, either now or in the future.

Let me know if you have any other suggestions.

We may want to return `filepath.SkipDir` (a type of `error`) here: https://pkg.go.dev/path/filepath#SkipDir so the walk can continue:

> The error result returned by the function controls how Walk continues. If the function returns the special value [SkipDir](https://pkg.go.dev/path/filepath#SkipDir), Walk skips the current directory (path if info.IsDir() is true, otherwise path's parent directory). If the function returns the special value [SkipAll](https://pkg.go.dev/path/filepath#SkipAll), Walk skips all remaining files and directories. Otherwise, if the function returns a non-nil error, Walk stops entirely and returns that error.

more info on this works: https://pkg.go.dev/path/filepath#WalkFunc

body:
The goal of this section of the code is to remove layers that aren't referenced by any manifest file. If we want to be conservative about not deleting data that could be referenced by an unreadable manifest then we can't delete anything if we have one bad manifest since in theory it could reference anything. In this case, we just abort the whole delete operation and there isn't a benefit to continue walking through the manifests.

If we want to be more aggressive about cleaning up the disk then the original code is fine. This has the benefit of avoiding potentially filling up the disk with uncollected garbage data but personally I would err on the side of not deleting data.

In theory we could be more aggressive about deleting data that was pulled from the internet and could be refetched but that opens up a bunch of additional questions and I don't think is really worth it for an edge case.

body:
I've seen a few folks mention using higher precision for keys and lower for values to balance the tradeoff.

These are my notes on it:

## K vs V cache quantisation

Precision Requirements:

- Keys are used in attention calculations to determine which parts of the input are relevant. This operation is more sensitive to precision loss.
- Values store the actual content to be retrieved. They can often tolerate more aggressive quantisation without significantly impacting model quality.

Efficiency:

- Key-query dot products in attention mechanisms benefit from higher precision to maintain accuracy in similarity calculations.
- Values are typically used in linear combinations, which are more robust to lower precision.

Memory Bandwidth Optimisation:

- Keys are accessed more frequently during inference (for every token generated), so keeping them in higher precision can reduce the need for frequent dequantisation.
- Values are only accessed when their corresponding keys are selected, allowing for more aggressive compression to save memory bandwidth.

Architecture Considerations:

- Some architectures (like MQA (multi-query attention)) use fewer keys than values, making it more feasible to keep keys in higher precision.
- The relative importance of keys vs. values can vary depending on the specific attention mechanism used.

```suggestion
When loading a new model, Ollama evaluates the required VRAM for the model against what is currently available.  If the model will entirely fit on any single GPU, Ollama will load the model on that GPU. If the model does not fit entirely on one GPU, then it will be spread across all the available GPUs.
```

I came to this conclusion (I'm not sure if it's 100% accurate):

head size = hidden_size/num_attention_heads

body:
Right, I've had my 6 hours of beauty sleep and am thinking clearly again 🤣 ,

I started to implement this but discovered it might not be the best approach. Here's why:

The `isEmbeddingModel` flag serves two distinct purposes:

1. In server.go/validation.go, it validates user input to ensure only f16/f32 cache types are allowed for embedding models
2. In estimateKvCacheSize, it ensures accurate memory calculations by forcing non-f32 cache types to f16

While we could try to force the cache type earlier, we need the memory estimation logic to "know" about embedding models to properly calculate memory requirements. If we removed the flag, we'd either have to duplicate the embedding model detection logic or potentially get inaccurate memory estimates.

I've kept the flag but improved the code by:
- Moving the validation logic to ValidateKVCacheType
- Simplifying the cache type handling in server.go
- Making the embedding model handling more explicit in estimateKvCacheSize

Let me know if I've misunderstood or if you see a better way we need to handle this!

body:
The primary place where check and queue partial characters is done is down below at line 513. For most cases, we won't call flushPending until we already have a full unicode character and the check here is a no-op.

There are two cases where we call flushPending with a potentially partial unicode character:
-  We've decided to end the sequence anyways - for example, we hit the character generation limit.
- We have data equal to a max unicode character (4 bytes) and the string is still invalid. This keeps us from queuing things indefinitely if there is a broken character that never gets completed.

In both of these cases, things are either getting sent or discarded so I just start chopping characters off the end until the string is either valid or empty.

The second case (max unicode size) may be a little problematic in rare cases where we have a valid string prefixing an invalid partial piece. As a result, I think I'm going to switch back to the open-coded unicode check that only looks at the end of the string.

I'll also add a comment in flushingPending with some more description.

body:
First pass at this and have some thoughts:
- I'm wondering if we could wrap this under the existing "options" parameter although that is meant for the model options and I'm not a fan of having the two conflated - it's something I'll try it out
- With this method we have to load the full model into the vRAM _and_ use the scheduler due to needing the tokenizer as well as the truncated content of the messages.
- There is a world where we can side load the model without the vRAM (like in the [tokenize draft PR](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/pull/8106/files#diff-829f94fd58de777429c6c25e68de745804cb600031e92995007fa08d7af32078R588-R601)). 
- We'd still have to refactor doing the truncation based on context length not in the runner and I think that's where we start bleeding scope.

My take is:
- Cleanup this PR - keep scope small and stick to this pattern for just using the scheduler for now
- Figure out more long term model loading + swapping for quick interactions vs loading into vRAM and have a shared interface for those common patterns

Not sure if you are referring to `cache` or `ctx` based on the quoted code.

`ctx` does need to be closed in the runner rather than here because otherwise the returned tensor is no longer valid after close.

`cache` has a `Close` function but we never really deallocate the model until the entire runner killed, at which point everything will be freed. I'm probably going to move the resource allocation for caches to the runner so that they can share memory better, which will also make it easier to cleanup everything at the same time. However, we still realistically won't free the memory until process exit.

body:
It's necessary because it is an interface, which itself contains a pointer. In this pass we go through:
 * An interface
 * A pointer to a concrete type
 * The concrete type

If we pass back the last one, setting to the original type (the interface) will fail because it is expecting a pointer.

This is essentially the same as what is currently being doing for non-interface pointers. However, there are now several different places where this conversion is done depending on the starting type, which is fairly confusing so I have updated the commit to consolidate them and also support additional combinations.
author: jessegross

body: `FullRuneInString` checks to see if there is a full UTF8 rune at the beginning of the string, whereas this is looking at the end. As a result, if we get back a token that has a valid UTF8 rune followed by an incomplete one, the library function will return true but ours will return false.

body:
I would rather store a sample.Sampler than spreading the sampling logic around everywhere, especially in `processBatch`, which is already too long. There's also no reason to recreate the sampling chain on every token. It's better to keep all of the sampling logic in `getTransforms`, though I would change the name back to something more general.

Besides readability, there is a more fundamental problem of what happens when you have stateful sampling? I think this is already a problem with the seed - the PRNG should only be seeded at the beginning of the sequence, not for every token.
author: jessegross

body:
I think there's two ways to go about it based on chats:
1. Sampler package stays extremely simple and the user of the package can handle the logic to figure out what things to run how
2. Sampler package takes all sampling parameters as a pass through and manages it there

As for things like seed - I was just looking into that. We might need to change some of the runner logic and how we're doing batching? There needs to be a way for us to map each sequence to its own sampler. 

The user can also change sampling parameters on a request level which means at minimum we need to create a new sampler on change aside from the sequence to sampler mapping.

body:
```suggestion
# Preventing Out of Memory (OOM) Errors

Ollama is designed to automatically manage memory usage and prevent out-of-memory errors. However, in some cases, these errors might still occur. Here are solutions to help prevent these crashes:

## Basic Solutions

1. Decrease Context Size
   - [Lower the `num_ctx` parameter](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/a4f69a0191b304c204ef074ccd6523f121bfddfe/docs/modelfile.md#valid-parameters-and-values:~:text=mirostat_tau%205.0-,num_ctx,-Sets%20the%20size)
   - This reduces how much text the model can process at once
   - Results in lower memory usage

2. Limit GPU Layer Usage
   - [Reduce the number of model layers that run on your GPU](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/6950#issuecomment-2373663650).
   - This helps balance the workload between GPU and CPU

## Advanced Solutions

For users who need additional control, the following environment variables can be configured:

- [`OLLAMA_GPU_OVERHEAD`](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/5f8051180e3b9aeafc153f6b5056e7358a939c88/envconfig/config.go#L237): Reserves additional GPU memory (e.g., for 512MB buffer)

body:
I think there is an issue because we are swapping the order of dimensions here but the actual mask data is still laid out in the original order:
https://github.com/dhiltgen/ollama/blob/1296b3999ec5d4c15f32f5ac8311da94cdb808c4/kvcache/causal.go#L243

This works for GGML because the mask is in its native format and we just swap the arguments of `FromFloatSlice` back. However, it's probably at least part of the cache drift issue in MLX since the mask is not actually row order.

Most of the other inputs (which are the ones that aren't in the backend's native format) are only a single dimension, so the order doesn't make a difference. However, the mask is 2D.

I think we should change the mask generation to be row order native and in GGML do a permute in `FromFloatSlice` and `FromIntSlice` for multidimensional tensors. For the mask specifically, we may not actually need a contiguous, which would make it fast, though that is probably not generically true for all inputs.

This way of using synchronized output is a bug.

Synchronized output mode is meant to be enabled per frame. What it does is to temporarily pause state updates. This code is requesting that the state never get updated through the entire duration of the progress bar. Fortunately, the terminal will just timeout the synchronized output mode and continue as normal, but that means that all this is accomplishing is delaying the first output until after that timeout period.

body:
It's subtle, but this change breaks synchronized output. Putting this flush at the end of the function instead of a defer statement means this line now runs _before_ the deferred `fmt.Fprint(p.w, "\033[?2026l")` call rather than after.

Previously, the terminal saw this:

```
... idle ...

\033[?2026h
<content update>
\033[?2026l

... idle ...
```

Now it sees:

```
\033[?2026h
<content update>

... idle ...

\033[?2026l
\033[?2026h
<content update>

... idle ...
```

Mode 2026 (ie "don't render updates") is now _on_ during the idle time rather than _off_ during the idle time. And the command to turn it off is immediately followed by a command to turn it back on. I'm not actually sure what a compliant terminal should do in this situation. On ghostty this causes the progress bar to not show up at all. On iTerm2 it causes the progress bar to only update in response to user inputs like clicks or keypresses, and otherwise remain static. Plausibly those terminals should do something more graceful. But in any case, better to arrange the flush to happen after `fmt.Fprint(p.w, "\033[?2026l")`, as before.

That's probably OK for logprobs since you need each token separately (though I would check what other APIs do). However, it's definitely an issue for normal use. We might want to move the Unicode handling in this function into the Ollama server so that it is closer to the API consumer where we know what we need.

There's another more subtle difference between the old and new code. The case is if the model generates a partial Unicode character and then continues with full Unicode characters without ever completing the partial. With the old code, we would truncate the string back to the last completely valid point. In the new code, we will pass through the broken Unicode as long as it isn't the last token.

body:
Embeddings generally require fully connected attention so prompt caching (and caching in general) don't really work.

We don't yet have any embedding models implemented for the Ollama engine. However, once we do, I would expect that they won't initialize a cache at all, causing the same effect of `cachePrompt == false`.

There is another reason to pass false here, which is that it can improve repeatability of results. People have asked for this and I think it is a reasonable request - one solution might be to automatically disable cache prompting and parallelism when temperature is 0 or a seed is set. However, that will hurt performance in those cases and we haven't implemented it yet.

I think at this point, you can simply remove the `cachePrompt` argument and code path.

body:
My thoughts were that we join the tempDir with all paths, and require they be absolute. Relative is awkward from the API perspective because it has no concept of a root directory. It just takes arbitrary file paths.

I think we take a stance one way or the other:

> NOTE: In either of the below, Ollama never attempts to coearce a path into the required form. Instead it rejects the whole request and nothing else happens.

**Absolute Paths only:**

- All paths in `files` MUST be absolute
- All paths are represented in the temp directory as `filepath.Join(tmpDir, absPath)`
- All joined temp paths are, as an added measure, checked with os.Root to ensure they, even at lower levels, are not attempting anything sly.

Examples:

```
/x/y/x (valid)
/a/b (valid)
/o/l/l/a/m/a (valid)

./x/y (invalid)
../x (invalid)
/a/../../b (invalid)
```

**Relative (rooted) Paths only:**

- All paths in `files` MUST be relative to `./`
- All paths will not start with `/` or `./` or `../` - `./` is implied.
- All paths MUST NOT start with a `.` or `..` or `/`
- All paths are represented in the temp directory as `filepath.Join(tmpDir, relPath)`
- All joined temp paths are, as an added measure, checked with os.Root to ensure they, even at lower levels, are not attempting anything sly.

Examples:

```
x/y/x (valid)
a/b (valid)
o/l/l/a/m/a (valid)

./x/y (invalid)
../x (invalid)
/y (invalid)
a/../../b (invalid)
```

body:
I agree with your assessment of the "Relative (rooted) Paths only" approach. Here's how I would clarify it:

### Relative (rooted) Paths only:

All paths in files MUST be relative to the current directory (without any traversal components):
- Paths MUST NOT start with "/" (absolute paths)
- Paths MUST NOT start with "./" or "../" (explicit current/parent directory references)
- Paths MUST NOT be just "." or ".."
- Paths MUST NOT contain traversal sequences anywhere ("/../", "/./") 
- Paths MUST NOT end with traversal components ("/..") or current directory references ("/.")
- All paths are represented in the temp directory as filepath.Join(tmpDir, relPath)
- All joined temp paths are, as an added measure, checked to ensure they remain within the base directory

### Valid Examples:
- "x/y/z" - Simple nested path
- "a/b" - Simple path with one directory
- "o/l/l/a/m/a" - Multiple nested directories
- "file.txt" - File in root
- "dir/file.txt" - File in subdirectory
- "a/b/" - Paths with trailing slash
- "a//b" - Paths with double slash (will be normalized)

### Invalid Examples:
- "/y" - Absolute path
- "./x/y" - Starts with current directory reference
- "../x" - Starts with parent directory reference
- "." - Current directory only
- ".." - Parent directory only
- "a/../b" - Contains traversal component
- "a/./b" - Contains current directory reference
- "a/../../b" - Contains traversal beyond boundaries
- "a/b/.." - Ends with parent directory reference
- "a/b/." - Ends with current directory reference

> Also, just to make sure it is clear: The provided paths (in whichever form we require) are always joined with the tmpDir BEFORE we pass to (*os.Root).Stat

This will not work since its an absolute path to the temp dir. `os.Root` rejects absolute paths. i've tweaked the logic to create/open the file through the root interface, which will properly validate containment regardless of whether the file exists or not.

Having it as part of the constructor is more natural but the intention is that it should be very rare that models need to set the config. In almost all cases, it will be set by the backend based on its specific requirements for fast attention.

The main reason for a model to set it is if they have a special version of attention that is not supported by our standard implementation and therefore they have written it themselves. In that case, they probably want the cache to behave in a standard way and not have based on the backend.

Given that, I didn't really want to clutter the constructor. We could have a second constructor for this case but it seemed nicer to keep the interface relatively consistent across caches.

body:
Currently this is an optional method of a backend so the most obvious way to avoid the type assertion is simply to make it a required part of the `Backend` interface. I was trying to reduce the number of things that backends need to do to get a minimal implementation up and running so I made it optional since it is mostly used for optimizations. However, a basic implementation is very simple, so it could go either way.

`BackendCacheConfig` is primarily used in conjunction with `ScaledDotProductAttention`, which is a separate, optional interface. So it might be nice to combine them into a single interface, however, `BackendCacheConfig` makes the most sense on a `Backend` whereas `ScaledDotProductAttention` goes on a `Tensor` so that doesn't look good. Plus they may not always be strictly linked.

I think this is a slightly different situation than `model.TextProcessor`, since that one is a required interface that needs a type assertion due to the struct design whereas `BackendCacheConfig` has a type assertion because it is optional.

I expect that the interactions between model, cache and backends will evolve over time as we have more of them and also more complex optimizations. I tried to keep the interface somewhat flexible but also not go too crazy trying to predict what we will need.

body:
I see your point about the slice behavior, but I believe there is still a bit of a  misunderstanding here.

Here's a blog post that articulates this better than me: https://www.sheddy.xyz/blog/modifying-slices-in-go
> While slices are indeed passed by value, this value is a reference to the underlying array. This means that modifications to the slice's contents within a function will be visible outside the function, even without using pointers.

The temperature function is only modifying the contents (token values) without changing the length or capacity. The first example in the blog shows an alternative pattern needed when using append() (which can potentially create a new slice), but our temperature function isn't doing that, it's just modifying existing elements.

So I still believe the pointer-to-slice in the temperature function is unnecessary in this case. Let me know if there's something I'm still missing here!

That is correct. This had retry/backoff in a previous iteration, but I removed it in favor of clients of the package retrying instead. Back-pressure is a wonderful drug.

However, in the current form, it will abort all in progress chunk downloads that are legit, and it seems aggressive to make the decision to terminate instead of letting the client decide. With that said, we can change it to update trace about the error, and let clients that want to fail fast cancel their context; otherwise it should not interrupt the valid progress being made, which is a win on retry because resumable downloads will prevent duplicate effort and the download will... well... resume.

body:
The reason I bring this up: I realized there isn't a single token or one-time prefix. E.g. the [cogito qwen models](https://ollama.com/library/cogito:3b-v1-preview-llama-q4_K_M/blobs/783adfd1d253) have tool calls that like this:

```
<tool_call>
{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": <args>}
</tool_call>
<tool_call>
{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": <args>}
</tool_call>
```

In other models, it might be

```
<tool_calls>[
{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": <args>},
{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": <args>},
]</tool_calls>
```

Perhaps some are simple:

```
[{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": <args>}, {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": <args>}]
```

Therefore I don't think we can rely on looking for a fixed "token" or even "prefix", as there are also:

* Text between tool calls
* Text after the tool call

Instead it seems like need to keep a request-level state of where we are in the tool calling template, so we can know when to parse json or python, or when to simply skip tokens. This part will be a bit tricky to get right (and maybe there's a simpler shortcut?). A shortcut could be to parse the prefix, then parse json or python, dismissing any tokens that don't parse as json or python properly (in between) until we're out of tokens.

I would challenge us to reduce this to 2 states instead of 9:
1. `prefix` (we are parsing the prefix or emitting content before it)
2. `calls` (parsing tool calls after the prefix)

In theory, that's all we need. If I understand right, there are 3 steps to parsing:

1. Stream tokens before the tool calling (e.g. `<think></think>` output)
2. Consuming the prefix if there is one (e.g. `<tool_calls>[`)
3. Consuming complete json objects until the response has finished

If we can reduce it down to 2 states, then it can be a boolean variable such as `found` which means we found the prefix.

body: Based on the [Win32 API docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/psapi/nf-psapi-enumprocesses#remarks), it looks like there's no way to known up front how large an array you need, it will just return up to the number you ask for, and wont fail if there are more.  So if there were > 2048, and the installer was past the 2048'th entry, we would incorrectly think it's not running (effectively same behavior as today.)  We could add logic to detect if there are 2048 entries, and if so, retry with a larger array.   Given the failure mode is relatively benign, I'm inclined to keep it simpler.

body:
The overall goal is to use UUIDs as much as possible to avoid this problem. Within the new engine we are able to do that in all cases except for rocm on Windows, which is also a case where we need to fall back to using ordinal identifiers today.

In the old engine (which is where this piece of code is from), we don't have a way of passing in those UUIDs. However, what we are doing here is enumerating the GPUs, getting their UUIDs to match up with the ones we want and then using the order as GGML sees it. Since GGML enumerates the devices once at initialization time and we are sharing that with llama.cpp, there should be no possibility of drift.

body: We sort the GPUs by free space descending before assigning, which is the same as what we do today. As a result, this will always use the second GPU here. Also it wouldn't fit in the first GPU (128MB free, 3*50MB required) and we prefer to schedule on the smallest number of GPUs.
author: jessegross

body:
In this case, the GPUs are from different vendors (cuda and rocm), so we will never mix them. The test case where we split across 2 GPUs is called "Multi GPU split".

Here we have 306 MB that we need to assign onto GPUs with 128 and 256 MB free. If they were the same vendor, we could use both GPUs and get 100% offloading. However, since we can't mix, we pick the one with the  highest VRAM, assign to that and spill the rest to CPU. If we had multiple GPUs from the same vendor then we would pick the vendor that allows us to offload the highest number of layers and split across those.

## Pull Request Overview

This PR adds the `OLLAMA_RUNNER_THREADS` environment variable to allow users to override the default CPU thread count for model execution. This provides fine-grained control for deployment optimization, particularly beneficial for dual Xeon servers where the automatic thread detection may not be optimal.

Key changes:
- Added `OLLAMA_RUNNER_THREADS` environment variable configuration with default value of 0
- Updated runner execution logic to check and apply the environment variable when set to a positive value
- Added comprehensive unit and integration tests to validate the new functionality

### Reviewed Changes

Copilot reviewed 4 out of 4 changed files in this pull request and generated 2 comments.

| File | Description |
| ---- | ----------- |
| envconfig/config.go | Added `RunnerThreads` configuration variable and documentation entry |
| runner/ollamarunner/runner.go | Integrated environment variable check to override default thread count |
| cmd/cmd.go | Added environment variable to CLI documentation list |
| runner/ollamarunner/threads_test.go | Added comprehensive test suite for the new thread configuration feature |

I don't think this is safe because it can trigger a computation that will rearrange the cache, invalidating the previous batch which is currently in flight. Even though there is a mutex around `ggml.Compute`, we trigger `activeBatch.computeStartedCh` before the computation actually starts. This means that there is a narrow race condition for the next batch to start being prepared before the previous started executing.

This also applies to `model.Forward`, which can trigger defrag, though that one can be eliminated if start using ggml_set_rows in the cache, which avoids the need to defrag.

This comment is no longer correct - the pending inputs are actually in the cache after calling Compute, which used to be part of Forward but is no longer.

There are some cases that I can think of that are related to this:
- Because we drop the mutex while doing computation, it's possible for incoming sequences to look at the values that we've added to the cache here and start relying on them before we've done the computation. This is OK as long as we ensure that this batch's computation happens before any future batch's and we never fail (unless we take down the whole runner). I think both of those are currently true but we need to be careful.
- Another possible issue is that the incoming sequence might match on the placeholder tokens and be incorrect when they get updated.

body:
I think there is probably an issue here for sliding window models that don't have any extra memory (such as gemma3). When we setup the next batch after the EOS, the sliding window will advance. However, since the follow on prompt doesn't have the EOS, we would expect a partial match. Partial matches break the cache for gemma3 since we haven't retained enough of the sliding window to support them. We have a check for this condition, so it should still work but be slow.

Everything seems to work currently and I wasn't able to quickly trigger it but I think there might be an issue lurking. We don't add pending inputs to `seq.cache.Inputs` for sequences that have been deleted - I'm not sure if this is a good thing since we don't really care about tokens after deletion or if it is masking an issue by having the metadata out of sync.

body:
To clarify, the race is `<ctx>.Compute(...)` could be called by something other than `computeBatch` before `computeBatch` does, due to way I have the channel set up, is that correct?

If that's correct, I'd propose a new Compute that looks something like this
```go
func (c *Context) ComputeWithNotify(cb func(), tensors ...ml.Tensor) {
	c.b.schedMu.Lock()
	defer c.b.schedMu.Unlock()
	go cb()
	...

then in `computeBatch` use that callback to send the channel signal so it happens after Compute has the lock and is running.

body:
It looks like everything is actually OK as it currently is (no bugs and no cache breakage).

When we run a batch through the cache, we need space for the batch plus the sliding window. This means that after we process an EOS token for gemma3, we actually have 1024 (sliding window) + 1 (EOS) tokens in the cache. Since we need 1024 tokens to be able to look back on, we actually have the ability to partial match on 1 less than the previous sequence, which works out perfectly for this case. Another way to think about it is that we are just overwriting and redoing the last batch when we get the next message.

So we can just remove the comment that you added about the gemma3 sliding window.

I don't think this is thread safe. This handler is running asynchronously from the processing thread. This means that we could be sampling at the same time that the grammar is changed. I think there are two potential consequences:
- The data structure update is not atomic - you might see the pointer change before the data that it is pointing to has been moved. In practice there are probably enough memory barriers from the other code but it's not robust to rely on those side effects.
- There might be some tokens that are processed before the grammar change is seen, so they don't follow the the required constraints.

body:
I believe there is a race here, accessing a seq after we are already done with it and potentially subtracting off sampling time that we didn't count in the first place:
- When we sample a token that happens to be a stop token, we will remove the sequence. This will signal the completion handler to send back the final stats in a separate go routine.
- We didn't know that this token was going to be a stop token, so we have already set up the next batch while this one was computing.
- When we process the post stop token batch, we will know that the sequence has already been removed and won't sample it or update `lastUpdatedAt`.
- We will update the `samplingDuration` for the sequence despite already having stopped the timer, racing against the completion handler.

Can we basically just keep the existing state machine and code path in `createLayout` and make that work for fully offloaded models? We could take the existing assignment logic (including quickly returning an empty set of GPULayers if there are no GPUs) and call that from a function which takes that result and applies the memory checks. This existing checks work for fully CPU layouts, they just get skipped currently.

I think this would help with two things:
- We want to evict loaded models based purely on free memory - not including swap. But if no other models are currently loaded then we can consider swap before refusing to load. We should do this for partial offload as well as full offload. I believe that the existing code handles this but the new one doesn't quite.
- The other component is the current state machine of probing the runner works for partial offload and should work for CPU only as well. It would be better to not introduce a special case for CPU only if we can avoid it.

body:
Conv3D applies bias without reshaping, unlike Conv2D which reshapes to `[1, 1, channels, 1]`. This inconsistency may cause broadcasting issues if Conv3D output layout differs from Conv2D. Consider documenting why Conv3D doesn't need reshaping or applying consistent reshaping for both.
```suggestion
		bias := m.Bias
		// Broadcast bias along spatial dimensions to match convolution output layout.
		bias = bias.Reshape(ctx, 1, 1, 1, 1, bias.Dim(0))
		t = t.Add(ctx, bias)
```

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Guard `done` channel from multiple closes in audio callback**

The PortAudio callback closes `done` whenever `len(recordedData) >= bufferSize`. After the first close, PortAudio may still invoke the callback until `stream.Stop` completes; any subsequent invocation will call `close(done)` again and panic with "close of closed channel", crashing the command. Track whether the channel has been closed (or send on it) before closing to avoid a race-induced panic.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.
author: chatgpt-codex-connector

body:
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Finalize WAV encoder before transcribing**

After writing audio frames to `encoder := wav.NewEncoder(...)` the code immediately calls `transcribeAudio("output.wav")` without ever calling `encoder.Close()` or closing the file handle. The WAV encoder writes the header and data sizes only when closed, so the file remains truncated and `wav.NewDecoder` in `transcribeAudio` will frequently return EOF. Close and flush the encoder (and the file) before attempting to read it back.

body: ## Pull request overview This PR raises the GPU discovery refresh timeout in `discover/runner.go` from 3s to 10s when the user has set `HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION`. On "unsupported" AMD GPUs forced via this env var, JIT kernel compilation / driver init for the refresh runner typically takes 4–6s, exceeding the previous 3s budget and causing the scheduler to fall back to stale (often zero) free-VRAM values — which in turn pushes subsequent model loads onto CPU. The change preserves the original 3s timeout for the default path. **Changes:** - Extend the existing-runner free-memory refresh timeout from 3s to 10s when `HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION` is set. - Apply the same conditional 10s extension to the bootstrap-fallback refresh timeout. - Emit debug logs noting that the env override was detected and the timeout was bumped. --- 💡 Add Copilot custom instructions for smarter, more guided reviews. Learn how to get started.

Consider adding a brief code comment explaining why 10s was chosen (e.g., JIT kernel compilation on overridden AMD GPUs typically takes 4–6s) and/or defining named constants, so a future reader understands the tradeoff and knows when it can be revisited. It is also worth noting that the underlying slow path (JIT compile / driver init) can affect users without `HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION` set as well (e.g. on natively-supported AMD GPUs under load); gating the longer timeout solely on this env var may leave similar timeout failures unaddressed for those users.

The `AccessControl` struct uses a map without any synchronization mechanism. If this is used in a concurrent context (which it is in the middleware), concurrent reads and writes to `allowedUsers` can cause data races and panics.

Consider using `sync.RWMutex` to protect access to the map:
```go
type AccessControl struct {
    mu           sync.RWMutex
    allowedUsers map[string][]string
}
```

Then use `ac.mu.Lock()` for writes and `ac.mu.RLock()` for reads in `GrantAccess` and `CheckAccess`.

type PluginManager struct {
    mu      sync.RWMutex
    plugins map[string]Plugin

Consider defining constants like MROPE_TEMPORAL_OFFSET, MROPE_Y_OFFSET, MROPE_X_OFFSET, MROPE_UNUSED_OFFSET.
```suggestion

	const (
		MROPE_TEMPORAL_OFFSET = 0
		MROPE_Y_OFFSET       = 1
		MROPE_X_OFFSET       = 2
		MROPE_UNUSED_OFFSET  = 3
	)

	for y := 0; y < ny; y++ {
		for x := 0; x < nx; x++ {
			i := y*nx + x
			tokenIdx := nTokensStart + i

			// Set M-RoPE positions with nTokensFinal as stride
			b.mropePos[tokenIdx+MROPE_TEMPORAL_OFFSET*nTokensFinal] = C.llama_pos(pos0)        // temporal
			b.mropePos[tokenIdx+MROPE_Y_OFFSET*nTokensFinal]       = C.llama_pos(pos0 + y)     // row (y)
			b.mropePos[tokenIdx+MROPE_X_OFFSET*nTokensFinal]       = C.llama_pos(pos0 + x)     // column (x)
			b.mropePos[tokenIdx+MROPE_UNUSED_OFFSET*nTokensFinal]  = 0                         // unused
```

body:
## Pull request overview This PR adds M-RoPE (Multi-dimensional Rotary Position Embedding) support for Qwen2-VL and Qwen3-VL vision models. M-RoPE uses 4 position values per token to encode 2D spatial information (temporal, y-coordinate, x-coordinate, and unused dimensions) for vision tokens, enabling these models to process images with proper positional encoding. Key changes: - Implements M-RoPE batch handling with 4-dimensional position encoding for image tokens - Updates model loading to support split model files - Adds repetition loop detection to prevent infinite generation loops - Increases batch size to 8192 for M-RoPE models to accommodate large images (up to ~4000 tokens) ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 5 out of 5 changed files in this pull request and generated 16 comments.
Show a summary per file | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | runner/llamarunner/runner.go | Adds M-RoPE batch processing, input tracking (imageNx/imageNy), position calculation, repetition detection, split model loading, resource cleanup, and flag library migration | | runner/llamarunner/image.go | Implements M-RoPE detection, adjusts batch size to 8192, updates embed size calculation to use NEmbdInp(), adds cache management | | runner/llamarunner/cache.go | Improves input comparison for embeddings, removes KV cache clearing for embeddings | | llama/llama.go | Adds NewBatchMRoPE() and AddImageMRoPE() methods, updates LoadModelFromFile for split models, adds NEmbdInp() accessor, implements 2D position encoding | | llama/patches/0032 | Patches llama.cpp to fix embedding dimension calculations for multimodal models (uses n_embd_inp instead of n_embd) |

body: Comparing slice backing array pointers (`&a.embed[0] == &b.embed[0]`) is unreliable for determining if slices share the same backing array. After re-slicing or garbage collection, the addresses can differ even for the same underlying data. A more reliable approach is to compare the slice headers using `unsafe.SliceData()` or compare data pointers directly with proper bounds checking.

body: The comment and code are both correct - there are two different functions with different stride strategies: Add() uses allocSize for single tokens, while AddImageMRoPE() uses nTokensFinal for the entire image batch. This is intentional because M-RoPE images must set all positions at once after knowing the final token count.
author: iosub

body: This is not a memory leak. The C strings must remain valid until llama_load_model_from_files() completes (which happens in this function before return). Using defer is correct here - it ensures cleanup happens at function exit, after the C function has finished using the strings. If we freed them at loop iteration end, the C code would access freed memory.
author: iosub

body: This is intentional and matches llama.cpp's mtmd_image_tokens_get_n_pos() implementation. For M-RoPE, temporal position advances by max(nx, ny), not nx*ny. This is because M-RoPE encodes x and y positions separately in different dimensions - the temporal axis is orthogonal to the spatial grid. See llama.cpp tools/mtmd/mtmd.cpp for the reference implementation.
